subject: philosophy
title: Deduction and induction
objective: Distinguish a guarantee from a well-supported expectation.

lesson.opening: These are introductory reasoning categories, not a complete taxonomy. Philosophers disagree about how best to draw their boundaries; explanations, analogies, and inference to the best explanation deserve further study.

sections.heading: Necessity and probability
sections.body:
A deductive argument aims to make its conclusion unavoidable if its premises are true. “Every key in this drawer opens the cabinet; this is a key in that drawer; so it opens the cabinet” makes a guarantee conditional on its premises. It may still fail because a premise is false.

An inductive argument supports a conclusion without ruling out its falsity. If a large and varied sample of the keys opens the cabinet, we may expect an untested key to open it. A defective key remains possible. Induction is often indispensable precisely because we act beyond what our evidence logically guarantees.

Do not define deduction as reasoning from general to particular and induction as reasoning from particular to general. A probability-based prediction about one case can be inductive; a mathematically valid argument can establish a general result. Here we classify the strength of support being claimed, not the direction of generality.

Good inductive evaluation asks about sample quality, relevant variation, and alternative explanations. A thousand observations from one biased source may support less than a carefully selected smaller sample. A failed deductive inference does not automatically become strong induction. We must ask whether its premises actually make the conclusion probable.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: Case A claims necessity relative to the premises. Case B expressly claims probability. The word representative matters: removing it weakens the inference if the sample is biased.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A critic asks why the observed sample should guide belief about unobserved cases. Merely collecting another sample does not by itself answer every version of this philosophical problem. In practice, we can still compare stronger and weaker sampling methods.

activities.prompt: Which conclusion can be false while its stated premises are true?
choices: B, because probability leaves room for an exception.

activities.prompt: Which change most improves a sample-based inference?
choices: Sample relevant subgroups and include failures.

activities.prompt: Three friends love a film, so everyone in the city will love it. The central weakness is…
choices: A small, unrepresentative sample and an overstrong conclusion.
Any reasoning about films is deductive.

activities.prompt: Which question targets the induction problem rather than a mere counting error?
choices: Why should observed regularities extend to unobserved cases?

activities.prompt: Can an inductive argument be valuable if its conclusion might be false?
choices: No: all useful reasoning guarantees truth.
Yes: strong evidence can support reasonable uncertain judgment.

activities.prompt: Does an invalid deduction automatically count as strong induction?
choices: No: its probabilistic support must be evaluated separately.

activities.prompt: Give one prediction you reasonably rely on without a logical guarantee. What evidence supports it, and what could undermine it?
activities.context:
Case A: Every sealed vial in tray A passed inspection. Vial 7 is a sealed vial in tray A. Therefore vial 7 passed inspection.
Case B: In a representative random sample, 98 of 100 vials passed inspection. Vial 8 comes from the same production run. It probably passed too.
rubric: I state a prediction rather than a certainty.
I give a possible defeating condition.
